findings.claim: the command stopped reading stdin at the first owned path, so under pipefail a long git diff got SIGPIPE and release-tag dropped an owned late commit

verdict.text: The command now reads all of stdin before it decides, so the writer in release-tag's pipeline is never cut off, and a new test pins this under pipefail.
Nothing else in the touched code regressed, and the gates are green.
`loopctl gate stamp` in the worktree: lint, format, tests, integration and rows r1, r2, r3 all pass; stamp green 803217b0dd146bb41b4c76c92e33623a9315c53f9ef18231eb0c7b2b49494d9e.
Read scripts/release_paths.py: `main` reads `sys.stdin.read().splitlines()` into a list, then applies `owns`; exit codes 0/1/2 match the docstring.

Reproduced the round 1 case against the new script: with `set -euo pipefail`, one docs path followed by 20000 kmaudit paths piped into `release_paths.py kmctl` takes the "owned" branch (it took "not" with exit 141 in round 1).
A kmaudit plus .okf input to kmctl still exits 1.

Read the new test test_the_command_reads_every_path_so_the_writer_never_dies_of_sigpipe: it runs the real script through `cat | python` under `set -euo pipefail` with about 500 KB of input, well past the pipe buffer, and asserts the `if` takes the owned branch.
Against the round 1 code the `cat` would die of SIGPIPE and the assertion would fail, so it covers the regression.
release-tag.yml's loop still pipes `git diff --name-only` into the script unchanged.
f1: resolved in scripts/release_paths.py:47-50, which drains stdin before deciding, and covered by the new pipefail test in tests/scripts/test_release_paths.py.
